interviewQuestions.question: How does Manacher's algorithm find the longest palindromic substring in O(n), and what does expand-around-center do wrong that makes it O(n²)?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Expand-around-center tries every possible center — n character centers for odd-length palindromes, n-1 gaps for even-length ones — and expands outward from each until a mismatch. That's correct, but on an input like all-identical characters, every single center expands almost the full length of the string, giving O(n²) total work.

Manacher's fixes this with two moves. First, it inserts a separator between every character (and at the ends) so every palindrome, odd or even, becomes odd-length in the transformed string — one uniform loop replaces the two separate cases. Second, and this is the actual speed win: it tracks the rightmost palindrome found so far, `[l, r]` centered at `c`. When computing the radius at a new position `i` inside that span, the mirror position `2c - i` has already had its radius computed, and by symmetry `i`'s radius is *at least* that value, capped at the boundary `r`. So instead of expanding from zero at every position, most positions start from an already-proven lower bound and only need to verify anything past it.

That reuse is what collapses the total work to O(n): every character is only ever re-compared past the point where it's already been proven to match, the same amortization argument as KMP's LPS fallback or the Z-array's Z-box.

**Testing:** whether you understand the mirror-reuse trick as the actual source of the speedup, not just that you've memorized "insert separators, get O(n)."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: Why does Manacher's algorithm insert separator characters into the string before processing it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Because a palindrome's center isn't always a single character. `"aba"` centers on the middle `'b'`; `"abba"` centers on the gap between the two `'b'`s — there's no index that's the middle. Without unification, you need two genuinely different expansion routines: one that starts from a character and checks both sides, and one that starts from a gap between two characters.

Inserting a separator (something guaranteed absent from the input, like `'#'`) between every character and at both ends converts every even-length palindrome into an odd-length one in the new string. `"abba"` becomes `"#a#b#b#a#"`, and its center is now the middle `'#'`, a real index — same shape as the odd-length case.

The payoff is that Manacher's needs exactly one expansion loop, one radius array, and one mirror-reuse rule, applied uniformly regardless of whether the original palindrome was odd or even length. The two-code-path version is where most naive implementations pick up subtle off-by-one bugs, usually in the even-length branch specifically, because it gets less test coverage than the more intuitive odd-length case — unification removes that entire bug surface by making both cases literally the same code.

**Testing:** whether you see the separator trick as solving a structural problem (no single-index center for even lengths), not as an arbitrary implementation detail.

interviewQuestions.question: In a coding interview, would you jump straight to Manacher's algorithm for a longest-palindromic-substring question?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
No — I'd start with expand-around-center and only bring up Manacher's if asked to push past O(n²), or if the interviewer signals up front that they want the optimal bound.

Expand-around-center is correct, quick to write cleanly (two small loops, one for odd centers, one for even), and demonstrates the exact same core insight — palindromes are found by growing outward from a center — without the extra bookkeeping Manacher's requires: separator insertion, tracking the rightmost boundary, the mirror-cap logic. For most realistic inputs (string lengths in the hundreds or low thousands, which covers the overwhelming majority of interview and even production use cases), O(n²) runs in microseconds, and reaching straight for the O(n) machinery reads as reciting a memorized algorithm rather than reasoning about the problem's actual scale.

I would proactively **name** Manacher's — "this is O(n²); there's an O(n) approach called Manacher's algorithm that unifies odd/even cases with separators and reuses palindrome symmetry, want me to implement that instead?" — which signals I know the ceiling exists without committing to riskier, harder-to-debug code unless the interviewer actually wants it. Jumping straight there is the same over-engineering mistake as reaching for a hash map to look up a 5-element list.

**Testing:** whether you calibrate solution complexity to what's actually being asked, rather than defaulting to the most "impressive" algorithm you know.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Trade-offs

interviewQuestions.question: Your Manacher's implementation passes on most test strings but returns a palindrome longer than actually exists in the original string on a specific repetitive input. How would you debug it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
This symptom — correct on typical inputs, wrong specifically on repetitive or highly-structured strings — is close to a signature bug: the radius-capping step being skipped or implemented wrong. I'd check first whether the code does `radius[i] = min(right - i, radius[mirror])` or the uncapped `radius[i] = radius[mirror]` directly.

The uncapped version is wrong exactly when the mirror position's palindrome would extend past the currently-known boundary `right` — the symmetry guarantee that justifies reusing the mirror's radius only holds *inside* the proven span `[l, r]`, so blindly copying a mirror radius that pokes past `right` inherits an unverified assumption. This bug tends to hide on random or short test strings, because it only manifests when a mirror's palindrome specifically reaches or exceeds the boundary — which needs enough internal repetition to construct, similar to how KMP's off-by-one hides until a pattern has real repeated structure.

I'd construct a minimal repro deliberately: a string engineered so a mirrored palindrome would overrun the boundary, something like `"aaaaaaaaaa"` or a crafted pattern with a long palindrome positioned to expose the cap. Running the buggy version against a brute-force expand-around-center on the same input and diffing the radius arrays index by index pinpoints exactly where they diverge, which should land right at the boundary-crossing position if the cap is the culprit.

Second thing I'd check, if the cap looks correct: the index math converting from the separator-padded string back to original coordinates — `(i - r) // 2` — since an error there can also silently report a palindrome slightly longer or shorter than reality without an obvious crash.

**Testing:** whether you can localize a subtle correctness bug to the specific invariant (boundary-capped mirror reuse) that a repetitive input is uniquely positioned to expose.
